cultivar: Gokou, Samidori, Saemidori, Okumidori (whatever the parent gyokuro or tencha was)
processing: The stems and leaf veins sorted out of gyokuro and tencha during refining, lightly fired; because the parent leaf was shaded for about three weeks, the stems carry the same amino-acid sweetness.
harvest_season: First flush only (May), because gyokuro and tencha are made only from the spring picking.
appearance_dry: Pale jade-green stems and petioles with a few dark gyokuro needles, lighter and greener than ordinary kukicha.
appearance_liquor: Pale green, clear, with a slight thickness.
appearance_wet: Soft, bright green stems and small shaded leaf fragments.
taste_profile: Sweet, round umami with a cool, almost sugarcane freshness and very little astringency; lighter and more refreshing than gyokuro itself.

brewing.notes: Treat it like a gentle gyokuro: cooler water and a longer first steep bring out the shaded sweetness; hotter water makes a perfectly good, lighter everyday tea. Stems are bulky, so weigh them.

vintage_note: Sold alongside the parent gyokuro as the current year's refining by-product, usually from early summer onward, and labelled 'gyokuro karigane' (or 'tencha karigane' when it comes from matcha production); Kyoto shops may also rest it like gyokuro and release it in autumn. Drink it within a year; it has no ageing value.
description:
Karigane is the Kyoto name for the stems sorted out of gyokuro and tencha, and it is the cheapest way to taste what shading does to tea. The parent leaf spent three weeks under cover storing theanine, and the stems carry the same sweetness and umami at a fraction of the price and with far less caffeine. The name means 'the cry of the wild goose' and is usually explained with a story about migrating geese resting on floating twigs; enjoy it as a story.

In gyokuro refining, the stems and petioles are separated from the needles by air and colour sorters; in tencha production they are removed before the leaf goes to the mill, because stems would ruin the colour of the matcha. Either way the stems are lightly fired and sold, and the better Kyoto shops treat them seriously, with grades and sometimes a cultivar on the label. In Kyushu the identical product is called shiraore.

Brewed like a gentle gyokuro, 6 g in a small pot with 100–120 ml of water at 60–65 °C for a minute and a half, it gives a pale, slightly thick cup that is sweet, cool and savoury, with a clean, almost sugarcane finish and none of gyokuro's density. Brewed hotter it becomes a lighter, everyday tea, and cold-brewed overnight it is a Kyoto summer classic. The one thing to avoid is expecting the thickness of the parent; it is a different, lighter experience.

Shops sell it as 'gyokuro karigane' or 'tencha karigane', sometimes with a grade, and it costs a little more than plain kukicha and far less than gyokuro. Look for pale jade-green stems with a few dark needles mixed in rather than brown, woody pieces, and ask what the parent tea was; a few shops use the word for sencha stems, which are not the same thing. It is a current-year product, often released in early summer and sometimes rested like gyokuro and sold in autumn.

If you like it, the next step is the parent: a Uji or Yame gyokuro from the same house.
